query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the effective in-flight powder mass flow (i.e. the powder feed rate) during HVOF spraying of the FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy will increase the as-sprayed bond coat thickness to meet design requirements while retaining the coating’s microstructural integrity and low oxidation levels.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock using standard HVOF parameters, which currently results in a deposit that is thinner than required for bond coat function.
generation.intervention: Increase the powder feed rate (i.e., deliver a higher mass of 15–45 μm feedstock per unit time) during thermal-spray HVOF deposition.
generation.conditions: Conduct the HVOF process under otherwise identical operating conditions (carrier gas composition, spray distance, substrate preheat, and chamber atmosphere) and service conditions typical of thermal barrier coating systems (e.g., elevated temperatures up to about 1000–1050 °C in an oxidizing environment).
generation.structural_mediator: A higher in-flight particle flux leads to increased particle impingement density and overlapping deposition, resulting in a thicker coating build-up. At the same time, by maintaining the same spray thermal and velocity conditions, the oxidation kinetics of individual particles remain constrained, preserving the formation of protective oxide phases (primarily α-Al2O3/Cr2O3) only at the surface.
generation.mechanism: By increasing the powder feed rate, the deposition efficiency is improved because more molten or semi-molten particles reach and adhere to the substrate per unit time, leading to a greater overall coating thickness. The elevated mass throughput reduces the dwell time of particles in the high-temperature environment such that the extent of in-flight oxidation remains minimal.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline 15–45 μm deposition, the increased feed rate is predicted to yield a bond coat with a significantly higher thickness (potentially 50–100% thicker, though the exact gain is uncertain) while preserving the dense microstructure and low as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.baseline: Deposition using current parameters with standard powder feed rate yields an insufficient bond coat thickness from 15–45 μm feedstock.
generation.boundary: The intervention should remain effective provided that other spray parameters (e.g., flame temperature, spray distance, and substrate preheat) are not altered to an extent that would lead to overheating or substantially longer particle dwell times. Excessive increase in feed rate that disrupts the optimal particle thermal history or deposition uniformity could negate the benefits.
generation.uncertainty: While the general mechanism is supported by studies on controlled particle oxidation and deposition efficiency in HVOF processes, the precise quantitative increase in thickness without adverse oxidation effects remains to be established experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of controlled HVOF depositions on identical substrates where only the powder feed rate is incrementally varied (e.g., in steps from the baseline up to a predetermined higher rate). For each run, record the coating thickness, in-flight particle temperature (if measurable), and oxidation state (by surface compositional analysis). The experiment should include replication to ensure statistical significance.
measurements: Coating thickness (via cross-sectional microscopy or profilometry)
Oxide content and phase identification (using XRD or Raman spectroscopy)
In-flight particle temperature or residence time (if available)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if increasing the powder feed rate does not produce a statistically significant increase in coating thickness relative to the baseline, or if the enhanced feed rate results in a detectable increase in as-sprayed oxidation (e.g., formation of undesired oxide phases or significantly higher oxide content) that compromises the coating integrity for service as a bond coat.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, in-flight oxidation of the AlCoCrFeNi particle during the spraying process can be beneficial for the tribological performance of the HEA coatings. Due to high specific surface area, the powder can oxidize differently from the cast bulk alloy. Moreover, the formation of multiple oxides—alumina, chromia, and spinel—changes the residual particle’s core composition and can lead to phase destabilization. Therefore, understanding the regularity of the oxidation behavior and phase transformation of the high-entropy powder at different conditions should be necessary for the production of a coating with high and determined property levels. In this work, the oxidation behavior and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder, produced via gas atomization, were studied. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and under prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 HVOF coatings were produced using various distances from the spray nozzle to the substrate to produce coatings with different oxide contents, and the coatings’ properties were investigated.

Oxidation and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder produced via gas atomization were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. The following was found:Under HVOF spraying, the processes of oxidation and phase transformations occur in the following sequence: (i) pronounced Al diffusion from subsurface BCC supersaturated solid solution to the particle surface; (ii) particle’s surface Al2O3 formation; and (iii) FCC formation in the Al-depleted subsurface layer.During continuous heating in an air atmosphere, processes occur in the following sequence: (i) decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma formation; (ii) Al diffusion to the surface; and (iii) simultaneous formation of Al2O3 and FCC due to Al outflow from BCC/B2.During prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C in an air atmosphere, processes occur in the following sequence: (i) decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma formation; (ii) diffusion of Al, Cr, Fe, and Mo to the surface; and (iii) formation of surface Al2O3 and undersurface sigma due to enrichment of the undersurface zone with Cr
